Subject: Intro + connectivity constraints for Solstice Pay POC

Hi Lukas / Kimberly —

Thanks for the intro call last week. As we scope the POC for Solstice Pay (payments processing), a few constraints we need you to consider for the Private deployment:

- PCI scope: customer data must not traverse the public internet; we need strong isolation and auditability.
- Latency: 95th percentile L2R token latency target < 50ms from our primary region (us-west-2).
- Throughput: initial sustained ~1200 TPS (small payloads) with bursts to 3500 TPS.
- Timeline: procurement wants a draft SOW and connectivity recommendation by next Wednesday (2026-09-23).

Can you outline pros/cons of three paths — VPC peering (cross-account peering), AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and site-to-site VPN (IPsec) — specifically in terms of security posture, operational complexity, latency characteristics, and cost drivers? Attached a rough network diagram (network-diagram.png) and our compliance checklist.

Also copying Elena from our infra team who will own procurement and testing.

Thanks,
Sanjay Rao
Head of Platform Engineering | Solstice Pay

From: lukas_meyer@redwood.com

Subject: Re: Intro + connectivity constraints for Solstice Pay POC

Sanjay — thanks for the clear constraints and the diagram. High level recommendation first: for your combination of strong isolation (PCI) and tight latency SLA, we recommend moving forward with AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) as the primary connectivity for the POC, with a Site-to-Site IPsec VPN as a documented fallback and peering considered only for controlled, low-LATENCY internal traffic where account routing and CIDR management permit.

Short rationale:
- PrivateLink (recommended):
  - Security: the model keeps traffic off the public internet and provides a provider-controlled endpoint in your VPC; simplifies audit because the endpoint mapping is explicit and integrates with VPC flow logs and PrivateLink resource policies.
  - Latency: typically a small extra hop but consistently low latency inside the provider fabric — for us we've measured 5–20ms overhead in most us-west-2 setups; predictable under load.
  - Operational: per-service interface endpoints scale horizontally, and Redwood can publish an ENI-backed endpoint per AZ to meet throughput targets.
  - Cost: per-hour and per-GB charges on AWS for the endpoint + data processing; economical vs expensive cross-region peering for high egress volumes but more than pure peering for high sustained throughput.

- VPN (fallback):
  - Security: encrypts over public internet; good as an auditable fallback for compliance tests.
  - Latency: variable and dependent on Internet paths; HA IPsec with BGP is possible but tends to have higher jitter vs PrivateLink.
  - Ops: simpler to set up quickly (useful for POC), but operational overhead increases at scale (monitoring, rekeying, throughput limits).

- VPC Peering (selective use):
  - Security: native routing between VPCs, no ingress endpoints — lower per-GB cost and low latency.
  - Constraints: cross-account peering requires non-overlapping CIDRs and careful routing; no transitive peering so multi-VPC topologies get complex. Also harder to lock down to a single service surface (more lateral exposure).

Next steps I propose:
1) We’ll produce a one-page connectivity decision matrix (latency, PCI posture, operational complexity, cost estimate) and a short runbook for PrivateLink + VPN fallback by EOD tomorrow.
2) Schedule a 45-min design review with your infra and network teams on Tuesday (2026-09-22) to agree on ENI placements, NAT considerations, and test plan.
3) Draft SOW with the connectivity appendix by Wednesday (2026-09-23).

Attaching a compact config snippet to show the PrivateLink ENI layout we typically use (privatelink-config-snippet.txt). Kim — can you add the HA ENI sizing and expected cost delta?

— Lukas

Thanks for the thread — adding a technical checklist and a few cautionary notes from the deployment/ops side. Quoting Lukas' summary below and augmenting with specifics.

On 20 Sep 2026 11:08, lukas_meyer@redwood.com wrote:
> PrivateLink (recommended): the model keeps traffic off the public internet and provides a provider-controlled endpoint in your VPC; simplifies audit because the endpoint mapping is explicit and integrates with VPC flow logs and PrivateLink resource policies.

Augmented checklist / notes:
- Throughput & ENI sizing: For 3.5k TPS bursts we expect to need multiple interface endpoints across AZs. Each ENI/iface has practical TCP session and throughput limits; we will recommend a minimum of 3 ENIs per AZ with load-balancing at the client side or use high-concurrency GOPs on the Redwood side.
- NAT & source IP: PrivateLink terminates at our service ENI — source IP visible to Redwood will be the endpoint ENI by default. If you need client source IPs preserved for logging in your infra, we will need to stitch via a separate direct peering path or implement a proxied header; this has PCI/logging implications to discuss.
- BGP/HA for VPN fallback: If we stand up IPsec fallback, set up dual tunnels to different endpoints with BGP and route priorities. Monitor tunnel jitter; recommend CloudWatch or third-party latency probes for cutover automation.
- MTU and fragmentation: IPsec tunnels reduce MTU; for payment payloads small but important — ensure path MTU discovery is validated in the test plan.
- Firewall rules & least privilege: limit Redwood ENI SGs to only the service ports required; recommend explicit deny-by-default rules in your firewall and allow lists in the PrivateLink policy.
- Cost expectations (order of magnitude): PrivateLink endpoint hourly + data processing (we’ll provide numbers), VPN data egress cheaper but incurs Internet variability, peering lowest per-GB but higher ops cost.

Proposed canary: start with a PrivateLink in a single AZ with synthetic load up to 1k TPS for 48h, verify 95p latency and failover behavior; then add AZs and ENIs to reach production target.

Lukas/Kim — I’ll add the sizing table and draft test plan into the Design Review doc.

— Ben Carter
Senior Network Engineer | Redwood Inference
